```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 3.5)
```

flexCountReg fits the same regression model with many count distributions.
This vignette is an overview of how to choose among them: which features of
the data matter, how to fit and compare candidate families on the same
rows, which comparisons are valid, and why some common shortcuts mislead.
For a first complete analysis start with
`vignette("getting-started", package = "flexCountReg")`; for the
diagnostics used here in more depth see
`vignette("diagnosing-count-models", package = "flexCountReg")`.

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
data("washington_roads")
```

## What to look at before choosing

A distribution is a statement about how counts vary *given the covariates*.
The useful questions are:

| Feature | Question | Families to consider |
|---|---|---|
| Conditional dispersion | Given the mean model, is the variance larger or smaller than the mean? How does it grow with the mean? | variance ∝ mean: NB1, PIG1, GP1, HERMITE; ∝ mean²: NB2, PIG2, PIG, PLN, NBGE; in between: NBP, PA |
| Underdispersion | Is the variance *smaller* than the mean? | COM, GP1/GP2, DW, DPO, HYPERPOIS, GAMMACOUNT |
| Tails | Are very large counts more frequent than a negative binomial allows? | PLN, PIG, SI, GW, PW |
| Zeros | Are there more zeros than the count distribution predicts *after* fitting it? | zero-inflated or hurdle models (`zero_formula`), PL, PLG, PGE |
| Exposure | Were the counts observed over different lengths of time or space? | any family, with an offset (`vignette("data-exposure-weights")`) |
| Mechanism | Is there a plausible process, e.g. events in clusters or batches, or renewal with regular gaps? | Polya-Aeppli (PA, clusters), HERMITE (pairs), GAMMACOUNT (renewal) |

`?count_families` lists every family with its parameters, variance and the
features (underreporting, likelihood-ratio tests) available for it.

## The data

The `washington_roads` data contain crashes on
`r length(unique(washington_roads$ID))` road segments, each observed in up to
three years (`r nrow(washington_roads)` rows). We model total crashes as a
function of traffic volume (`lnaadt`) and the speed-limit indicator
`speed50`, with the logarithm of segment length as an offset. The models in
this overview treat every row as independent; the repeated observations of
the same segments are modelled in
`vignette("random-parameters-and-panels", package = "flexCountReg")`.

## Fitting candidate families on the same rows

`countreg()` takes the distribution as `family`. Gradient-based optimizers
(`method = "BFGS"` or `"NR"`) are usually the fastest choice for the
closed-form families.

```{r fits}
f <- Total_crashes ~ lnaadt + speed50
fit <- function(family) {
  countreg(f, data = washington_roads, family = family, offset = "lnlength",
           method = "BFGS")
}
models <- list(
  Poisson = fit("Poisson"),
  NB1 = fit("NB1"),
  NB2 = fit("NB2"),
  PIG1 = fit("PIG1"),
  GP1 = fit("GP1"),
  PA = fit("PA"),
  DELAPORTE = fit("DELAPORTE")
)
sapply(models, nobs)
```

All models use the same rows, so their log-likelihoods are comparable. NB1
and NB2 differ in how the extra variance grows with the mean; the
Polya-Aeppli family `PA` (a Poisson-Tweedie distribution, variance
$\mu + \phi\mu^{1.5}$) lies between them, and the Delaporte family mixes a
Poisson and a negative binomial component.

## Comparing fit statistics

`glance()` gives one row of fit statistics per model:

```{r glance}
stats <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(nm) {
  cbind(model = nm, glance(models[[nm]])[, c("logLik", "AIC", "BIC", "df")])
}))
stats$dAIC <- stats$AIC - min(stats$AIC)
stats[order(stats$AIC), ]
```

```{r best, include = FALSE}
ord <- stats[order(stats$AIC), ]
close <- ord$model[ord$dAIC < 2]
nb1_gap <- min(stats$dAIC[stats$model %in% c("NB1", "PIG1", "GP1")])
```

`r ord$model[1]` has the lowest AIC, but
`r if (length(close) > 1) paste0(paste(close, collapse = ", "), " are within 2 AIC units of each other, a difference too small to choose between them on this basis alone") else "no other model is within 2 AIC units"`.
The families whose variance is proportional to the mean (NB1, PIG1, GP1)
are at least `r round(nb1_gap, 1)` AIC units behind the best model: the
extra variance grows faster than the mean in these data.

More parameters can also be weakly identified. The Delaporte model's
share and shape parameters have large standard errors here:

```{r delaporte}
summary(models$DELAPORTE)$coefficients[c("logit(rho)", "ln(k)"), 1:2]
```

The data do not separate the Poisson and negative binomial components of
the Delaporte distribution; it offers no advantage over NB2.

## Which comparisons are valid

For a single model, `summary()` reports a likelihood-ratio test against the
Poisson model with the same mean specification, when Poisson is a special
case (on the boundary of the parameter space for NB2, so the p-value uses a
50:50 chi-square mixture):

```{r summary}
summary(models$NB2)
```

`regCompTest()` compares two fitted models. Poisson is nested in NB2:

```{r lrtest}
regCompTest(models$Poisson, model2 = models$NB2)$statistics
```

NB1 and NB2 are not nested (neither is a special case of the other), so no
likelihood-ratio p-value is reported, only information criteria:

```{r not-nested}
regCompTest(models$NB1, model2 = models$NB2)$statistics
```

`regCompTable()` builds a coefficient table across models:

```{r table}
regCompTable(models[c("Poisson", "NB1", "NB2")])
```

McFadden's pseudo R-squared compares each model with the same baseline, an
intercept-only Poisson model, so the values are comparable across
distributions. A different baseline can be chosen with the `basemodel` and
`variables` arguments of `regCompTable()` and `regCompTest()`.

## Shortcuts that mislead

Three summaries are often used to choose a distribution before fitting
anything. None is sufficient on its own:

```{r shortcuts}
y <- washington_roads$Total_crashes
pearson <- function(m) {
  sum(residuals(m, type = "pearson")^2) / (nobs(m) - length(coef(m)))
}
expected_zeros <- sapply(models[c("Poisson", "NB2")], function(m)
  mean(predict(m, type = "prob", max_count = 0)[, 1]))
c(variance_to_mean = var(y) / mean(y),
  pearson_poisson = pearson(models$Poisson),
  observed_zeros = mean(y == 0),
  expected_zeros_poisson = expected_zeros[["Poisson"]],
  expected_zeros_nb2 = expected_zeros[["NB2"]])
```

* **The unconditional variance-to-mean ratio**
  (`r round(var(y) / mean(y), 2)`) mixes the variation explained by the
  covariates with the variation left over. After fitting the covariates the
  Poisson Pearson dispersion is `r round(pearson(models$Poisson), 2)`: there
  is overdispersion, but less than the raw ratio suggests.
* **A large share of zeros**
  (`r round(100 * mean(y == 0))`% here) is not evidence of a separate zero
  process: the fitted Poisson model already expects
  `r round(100 * expected_zeros[["Poisson"]])`% zeros. Compare the observed
  zeros with those expected under the fitted model.
* **An AIC ranking** tells which of the fitted models is closest to the data
  among those tried. Small differences are not decisive, and a model that is
  best in-sample is not necessarily best at predicting new data; a
  held-out comparison is shown in
  `vignette("diagnosing-count-models", package = "flexCountReg")`.

## Does the model reproduce the counts?

Information criteria rank models, but they do not show *where* a model
fails. A rootogram compares the observed frequency of each count with the
frequency expected under the fitted model, on a square-root scale. Bars hang
from the expected curve; a bar that ends above zero means the count is
over-predicted, one that ends below zero means it is under-predicted.

```{r rootograms}
oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
rootogram(models$Poisson, main = "Poisson")
rootogram(models$NB2, main = "NB2")
par(oldpar)
```

Randomized quantile residuals are approximately standard normal when the
model is correct, for any count distribution, so a normal Q-Q plot is a
useful check (the residuals are randomized, so a seed is set):

```{r qq}
set.seed(1)
oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
for (nm in c("Poisson", "NB2")) {
  r <- residuals(models[[nm]], type = "quantile")
  qqnorm(r, main = nm, pch = 20, col = "grey40")
  abline(0, 1, lty = 2)
}
par(oldpar)
```

A CURE plot (cumulative residuals against a covariate) checks the mean model
along that covariate; its bounds assume independent residuals:

```{r cure, message = FALSE, fig.height = 3}
cureplot(models$NB2, indvar = "lnaadt")
```

## Modeling the dispersion and the zeros

The distribution parameters can depend on covariates. Here the NB2
dispersion depends on the speed-limit indicator:

```{r generalized}
nb2_gen <- countreg(f, data = washington_roads, family = "NB2",
                    offset = "lnlength",
                    dis_param_formula_1 = ~ speed50, method = "BFGS")
tidy(nb2_gen, conf.int = TRUE)
```

When there are more zeros than a count distribution allows, a zero-inflated
or hurdle version of any family can be fitted with `zero_formula`:

```{r zinb}
zinb <- countreg(f, data = washington_roads, family = "NB2",
                 offset = "lnlength", zero_formula = ~ 1, method = "NR")
pi_zero <- unname(plogis(coef(zinb)["Zero:(Intercept)"]))
c(NB2 = as.numeric(logLik(models$NB2)), ZINB = as.numeric(logLik(zinb)),
  zero_probability = pi_zero)
```

The estimated probability of a structural zero is
`r format(signif(pi_zero, 2), scientific = TRUE)` and the log-likelihoods
differ by
`r format(signif(abs(as.numeric(logLik(zinb) - logLik(models$NB2))), 2), scientific = TRUE)`:
the zeros
are already explained by the negative binomial, so the zero-inflated model
adds nothing. When an estimate is at the boundary of its parameter space
like this, its standard error is not meaningful, and the likelihood-ratio
test of NB2 against ZINB has a non-standard distribution, so it is not
reported.

## Using the chosen model

Predictions have one value per row of new data. Besides the expected count,
`predict()` gives the probability of each count and confidence or prediction
intervals:

```{r predict}
nd <- washington_roads[1:3, ]
predict(models$NB2, newdata = nd)
round(predict(models$NB2, newdata = nd, type = "prob", max_count = 4), 3)
predict(models$NB2, newdata = nd, interval = "prediction", level = 0.9)
```

Marginal effects (or elasticities) on the expected count come from
`margEffTable()`:

```{r margeff}
margEffTable(models$NB2)
```
